highlights.title: Highlights
highlights.description:
Conway's refinement conjecture asks whether every equality $ab=cd$ of omnific integers can be refined as $a=ef$, $b=gh$, $c=eg$, $d=fh$ with omnific integers $e,f,g,h$. For an integral domain this is the pre-Schreier property: every element is primal. Conway normal form, with the signs of the exponents reversed, identifies the omnific integers with a ring of the form $\mathbb Z+\mathbb R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$, so the question becomes one about factorisation of generalised power series.

The algebraic core is a statement about Berarducci's ring of germs. Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero, $G$ an ordered abelian group that is Cauchy complete, and $J$ the ideal of series in $K((G^{\le0}))$ whose support is bounded away from $0$. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma\le0$ is the class modulo $J$ of the translated truncation $b^{|\gamma}=t^{-\gamma}b_{|\gamma}$ [Ber00, Def. 6.1]. Germs satisfy Berarducci's convolution formula [Ber00, Lem. 7.5], and the Cantor--Bendixson rank of $0$ in the closure of the support strictly decreases when $b$ is replaced by $b^{|\gamma}$ for $\gamma<0$ sufficiently close to $0$. From these two facts one transcendence lemma follows: if a subalgebra $S$ of $K((G^{\le0}))/J$ is an integral domain and every element of $S$ is the germ of a series all of whose germs lie in $S$, then the germ of a series whose germs at negative exponents lie in $S$, but which is not itself in $S$, is transcendental over $S$. Adjoining germs of minimal rank by transfinite recursion presents $K((G^{\le0}))/J$ as a polynomial ring over $K$; in particular $J$ is prime and the ring of germs is a unique factorisation domain. For real exponents the same recursion, carried out on series instead of germs, presents $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ as a polynomial ring over its subring of series with finite support. Hence $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a GCD domain and every element is primal.

The general ring $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ is reduced to these two theorems along the Archimedean classes met by the support of a series. Both cases rest on one step: regrouping along a convex subgroup $C$ presents the ring as a $D+M$ construction over the quotient $G/C$. Finitely many classes are handled by induction, taking $C$ below the leading class, where the quotient is $\mathbb R$. When the support meets infinitely many classes, primality in the ring of germs over the quotient of $G$ by a convex subgroup, combined with restriction of supports to convex subgroups, gives primality by transfinite induction on the order type of the set of classes. For saturated exponent groups and for surreal exponents, a cut criterion supplies the required Cauchy completeness, and signed Conway normal form carries refinement back to the omnific integers.

phases.title: Germs of translated truncations
phases.description:
Let $K$ be a field and $G$ a nontrivial ordered abelian group, and let $J$ be the ideal of series in $K((G^{\le0}))$ whose support is bounded away from $0$. For a series $b$ and an exponent $\gamma$, the germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is the class modulo $J$ of the translated truncation $b^{|\gamma}=t^{-\gamma}b_{|\gamma}$ [Ber00, Def. 6.1]. This chapter records the four properties of germs on which everything else rests. When $G$ is Cauchy complete for its order topology, the germs of a product obey Berarducci's convolution formula, a finite sum over the decompositions $\gamma=\xi+\zeta$. The germs of $b^{|\xi}$ are the germs of $b$ translated by $\xi$. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is nonzero exactly when $\gamma$ lies in the closure of the support, and the germ at $0$ is a constant exactly when the germs at all $\xi<0$ sufficiently close to $0$ vanish.

The complexity that makes inductions possible is the Cantor--Bendixson rank of $0$ in the closure of the support. It is zero on $J$, it depends only on the germ, and for a series whose germ is not a constant it strictly decreases when the series is replaced by its translated truncations at all exponents $\xi<0$ sufficiently close to $0$. The next chapter uses only these properties.

phases.title: Polynomial presentations
phases.description:
The properties of the preceding chapter are first isolated as axioms on a ring of series $A$ over a field $K$ of characteristic zero, with germ maps into a ring of germs. Fix a subalgebra $S$ of the ring of germs such that every element of $S$ is the germ of a series all of whose germs lie in $S$, and a series $X$ whose germs at negative exponents lie in $S$ while its germ $x$ does not. Applying the germ maps at negative exponents to a relation $ax+b=0$ and inducting on the Cantor--Bendixson rank of $a$ shows that no nonzero $a\in S$ has $ax\in S$. If $S$ is an integral domain, a polynomial relation for $x$ over $S$ of minimal degree is pushed through the germ maps; comparing the coefficients of the two highest powers of $x$, and using that $K$ has characteristic zero, reduces it to a relation of degree one between two series whose germs near $0$ are proportional, and an induction on rank excludes such proportionality. Hence $x$ is transcendental over $S$, and $S[x]$ again has the representative property.

Transfinite adjunction of germs of minimal rank then presents the ring of germs $K((G^{\le0}))/J$ as a polynomial ring over $K$ for every Cauchy-complete ordered abelian group $G$; each intermediate stage is a polynomial ring and therefore an integral domain. Consequently $J$ is prime. For real exponents, the series whose germs are all constants are exactly the series with finite support, and the same adjunction carried out with subalgebras of series closed under truncation presents $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ as a polynomial ring over its finite-support subring $K(\mathbb R^{\le0})$. Since $K(\mathbb R^{\le0})$ is a GCD domain, the multivariate Gauss lemma makes $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ a GCD domain, so every series is primal and every irreducible series is prime. The following chapters use this primality theorem for each Archimedean class and the polynomial presentation of the germ ring for the limit step.

phases.title: Finitely many Archimedean classes
phases.description:
Let $G$ be an ordered vector space over an Archimedean ordered field, $R$ a field of characteristic zero, $Z\subseteq R$ a pre-Schreier subring and $\kappa$ an uncountable regular cardinal. The ring of interest is $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$, the series of support size less than $\kappa$ with nonpositive exponents and constant term in $Z$. For a convex subgroup $C$ of $G$, regrouping exponents along $C$ writes this ring as the $D+M$ construction $D+L((\Gamma^{<0}))_\kappa$ inside $T=L((\Gamma^{\le0}))_\kappa$, where $\Gamma=G/C$, $L=R((C))_\kappa$ and $D=Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$, and the constant coefficient of a regrouped series is its restriction to $C$. The $D+M$ lemma therefore makes a series primal as soon as its regrouping is primal in $T$, its restriction to $C$ is primal in $D$, and $L$ is the fraction field of $D$ when that restriction vanishes.

For a series with nonzero lowest exponent, let $\sigma$ be the Archimedean class of that exponent and take $C=G_{\prec\sigma}$. The support lies in $G_{\preceq\sigma}$, whose image in $G/C$ is identified by a complement $H_\sigma\cong\mathbb R$ with $\mathbb R$; since primality in a convex exponent subgroup passes to the ambient ring, the regrouped series is primal by the primality theorem for real exponents of the previous chapter. The restriction to $C$ meets fewer classes, and the cofinality assumption makes $L$ the fraction field of $D$, so induction proves primality whenever the support meets only finitely many Archimedean classes.

phases.title: Transfinite induction on Archimedean classes
phases.description:
If the support of $x\in Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ meets infinitely many Archimedean classes, the well-ordered set of these classes splits into an infinite initial segment $T$ without least magnitude and a finite final segment. Let $C$ be the convex subgroup of exponents whose Archimedean class is smaller than every class in $T$, and $\Gamma=G/C$. Regrouping exponents along $C$ writes the ring as $D+L((\Gamma^{<0}))_\kappa$ with $D=Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$ and $L=R((C))_\kappa$. The constant coefficient meets only the finitely many final classes, so it is primal by the preceding chapter, and primality through regrouping reduces the problem to primality in $L((\Gamma^{\le0}))_\kappa$.

There, an abstract criterion combines two pieces of information. If $\Gamma$ is Cauchy complete, the ring of germs of $\kappa$-bounded series is a polynomial ring over $L$, so every germ is primal. Restriction of supports to a convex subgroup of $\Gamma$ is a ring endomorphism that tests divisibility, and every series factors as its restriction to the closed ball of a class met by its support times a cofactor with constant coefficient $1$ whose classes have strictly smaller order type. Transfinite induction on this order type then proves that every element is primal, provided the quotients $G/C$ are Cauchy complete and $R((C))_\kappa$ is the fraction field of $Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$. The chapter ends with the converse observation that refinement forces $R$ to be the fraction field of $Z$. The remaining chapters verify the two hypotheses for saturated groups and for surreal numbers.

phases.key: A cut criterion for Cauchy completeness
phases.title: A cut criterion for Cauchy completeness
phases.description:
The transfinite induction needs the quotients $G/C$ to be Cauchy complete. In the applications, the available hypothesis is about order: two small separated families have an element between them. This chapter turns that ability to fill cuts into Cauchy completeness.

Start with a Cauchy filter and choose points in sets of successively smaller diameter. The chosen points give the lower and upper sides of a cut. A point filling the cut lies within twice each chosen scale, so the filter converges. The chapter also shows that a monotone surjection which reflects strict inequalities passes cut filling to the quotient. This lets the same criterion handle both saturated ordered groups and surreal numbers.

phases.title: Bounded generalised-power-series integer parts
phases.description:
The transfinite theorem is now applied to a $\kappa$-saturated ordered rational vector space $G$. Saturation makes every Archimedean stratum isomorphic to the ordered additive group of real numbers, and gives the cofinality needed for the closed and open balls of Archimedean classes and for the convex subgroups $C$ of the preceding chapters. By the cut criterion each quotient $G/C$ is Cauchy complete, and the cofinality of $C$ gives the fraction-field property of $Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$.

This checks every hypothesis used by the reduction and the transfinite induction. If the coefficient subring is pre-Schreier, then $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ is pre-Schreier and has the refinement property. Taking $Z=\mathbb Z$ gives the corresponding theorem for $\mathbb Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$. No facts about surreal numbers have been used yet. The last chapter proves the same properties for surreal exponents in a different way.

phases.title: Surreal numbers and omnific integers
phases.description:
The last step connects the general series theorem to omnific integers and checks its hypotheses for surreal exponents. Conway normal form gives a ring isomorphism after the exponents are negated. Under this isomorphism, omnific integers become bounded series with nonpositive surreal exponents and an integer constant term, so the algebraic problem can be solved for series and the answer carried back.

Every nonzero surreal Archimedean stratum is isomorphic to the ordered additive group of real numbers. Conway's simplicity theorem for small cuts gives the required cofinality statements and fills small cuts. The cut criterion then makes the quotients by the relevant convex subgroups Cauchy complete, while cofinality gives the fraction-field property. The transfinite theorem shows that every element of the corresponding integer part is primal and hence has the refinement property. Conway normal form carries this refinement to the omnific integers, and the equivalence with Conway's cut definition gives the final theorem.
